product_meta.title: Beethoven: Symphonies No 1 & 3
product_meta.store: Ludwig van Beethoven  (Composer),     Hermann Scherchen  (Conductor),     Vienna State Opera Orchestra  (Orchestra),     Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London  (Orchestra)    &                   1                  more   Format: Audio CD

user_history.review_text:
Hermann Scherchen was the echt- and arch-radical. Based on these recordings of Beethoven's Symphonies 1, 3, 6 and 8, made between 1954 and 1958 and originally published on Westminster, he had a unique way with this composer as well. There had been Toscanini and others, but this is far more radical, and way ahead of its time - only with Norrington's "historically-informed performances" did I encounter such radical readings ([[ASIN:B000002RRB Symphonies 1-9]]), Leibowitz's pioneering cycle from 1961 included.

The reissues of Scherchen's Westminster cycle on CD are a tricky affair. He recorded the complete cycle between 1951 and 1954 with the Vienna State Opera Orchestra (1, 3, 6, 7, 9) and the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra (dubbed for contractual reasons the "Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London": 2, 4, 5, 8). He rerecorded 3 and 6 in stereo in 1958 with the VSOO, and, along with the 1954/RPO recordings of 1 & 8, it is those stereo remakes you get here, in this MCA release from 1988. It is the same that were reissued, in refurbished sound, by DG when they took over the Westminster catalog: [[ASIN:B00005OLDP Beethoven: Symphonies Nos. 3 & 6]]. The complete Westminister cycle was reissued by Universal Japan under the Westminster label, but those discs were not circulated in the West (I have 4+5, 1+the 1953 Eroica, and 9). Recently, Tahra published a complete set with the earlier version of the 6th - but NOT the 1953 Eroica: they used instead a previous recording from 1951, made for the label Ultraphon with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra ([[ASIN:B002C8BQZQ Beethoven: Complete Symphonies Vol. 1; Symphonies Nos. 1- 4]], [[ASIN:B002C8BR00 Beethoven: Complete Symphonies, Vol. 2, Symphonies Nos. 5-8]], [[ASIN:B002C8BR0A Beethoven: Complete Symphonies, vol. 3 : Symphony No. 9]]). Note also that the MCA discs under review came in the enjoyable "twofer" collection (I need to do a listmania of that some day), which had two companion CDs not in a multi-CD jewel case but in two different, standard jewel cases, which made it easy to sever them from each other. Hence, many are sold on this website separated from their legimitate companion, which might be the case with this entry, so make sure to check with the seller before you commit. You will find the companion under [[ASIN:B00000DWBD Beethoven: Symphonies Nos. 6 "Pastorale" & Symphony No. 8]], and there's also a listing for the complete set under [[ASIN:B000K6RTR6 Herman Scherchen. Beethoven Symphony 1 3 6 8 Vienna State Opera Orchestra]]. That said, with the Tahra reissues and the DG/Westminster 3 and 6 in much improved sound (the MCA is more than acceptable but suffers small, occasional drop outs, and the DG/Westminster reissue has done wonders in removing a lot of tape hiss and giving the orchestra a fine tonal bloom), these MCA discs aren't as indispensable as they were (if you can find the DG/Westminster at an affordable price!); but they were those I cherished for years.

It is good that MCA decided for the two stero remakes of the Eroica and Pastorale, and not just for sonic reasons. They are far more radical. These readings will shock. The first movement of the Eroica (with repeat) is the fastest I've encountered before Norrington. The first movement of the Pastorale is not an "awakening of happy feelings upon arrival in the country side", it's an explosion of joy, a bacchanal of joy, the suburban kids seeing the ocean for the first time in their lives. Scherchen's brook isn't the stagnant pond made out by many slower readings - it really flows, it's not a brook, it's a stream, maybe a small cascade.

All this will no doubt seem impossibly fast to those nurtured on another tradition, but in fact, Scherchen takes those movements exactly at (first movement of the Pastorale) or almost at Beethoven's controversial metronome marks (a little slower or a little faster) and - unlike Toscanini, but like Norrington - never relents. As hinted, in the first two movements of the Pastorale I find it jarring maybe, but ultimately uplifting. In the Eroica it is not entirely convincing, if only because Vienna State Opera Orchestra is obviously not a virtuoso ensemble, and THEY certainly feel hard-pressed, at times scrambling to keep together and at times lacking the lilt so typical of the rapid 3/4 time signature (Norrington is much more dance-like here), but there's no denying the high-octane energy and excitement Scherchen generates. His funeral march on the other hand I find an extraordinary experience. He sets off at a brisk tempo, that again will shock those raised on Furtwängler and old Klemperer, but still slower than Beethoven's metronome mark (circa 70 to Beethoven's 80 - for the metronomic tempo go to Norrington), although he does accelerate to Beethoven's tempo and faster in the climactic "Minore" section. The result of this faster tempo, added to Scherchen's sharp accenting and care for instrumental detail, is, I find, illuminating: you never get the sense that it is "fast", but it conveys gripping drama and also a real sense of a march. These days when our beloved ones are conveyed to their last repose in big limos, many conductors (or shall I say drivers?) seem to have forgotten what exactly is a funeral MARCH: they smoothen it out. Not Scherchen. For the first time I felt that the fugato in the "Minore" section at 6:23 (where Scherchen accelerates to a phenomenal 92 eighth-notes/mn) sounded just right, grippingly intense and angst-ridden, rather than like an overblown Bach arrangement by Stokowski. And for those who like their Beethoven to be turned to the future and not the past and a harbinger of things to come, never have the funeral bass triplets sounded to me more evocative of the march that opens Mahler's Fifth Symphony, and of Mahler's 2nd Symphony when they invade the full string section, underpinning ferocious brass utterances at 8:30.

Scherchen takes the scherzo (I'm still in the Eroica) at a slightly faster tempo than Beethoven's metronome (and the same as Szell) and invests it with great power (the first ff erupts at 0:46, brass with all bells up, to exhilarating effect) and instrumental pungency. It is in the finale that I find Scherchen's approach the most disputable. He hurls into the first bars with headlong fury, and it is very impressive, but from there he never relents: it takes him 5:27 to get through the first, "allegro molto" section, compared to Toscanini's 6:17, and Furtwängler's... 7:11. This is certainly a one-sided view of the music, hard-driven, suffocating even, with no time for breathing or supple dancing. If it were a dance it would be a dance of the elves on a bacchanale (another one!), but here the elves are gone berserk. But again there is no denying the high-strung excitement it generates. AND - Scherchen is still slower than Beethoven's metronome (circa 72 to Beethoven's 76 half-notes/mn, although he does reach and overpass the mark in the fugato section starting at 2:20). And kudos to all the performers. The blowers must have been on cocaine. By contrast the penultimate section, "poco andante", starting at 5:27 (and here Scherchen is very much a traditionalist, with a quarter-note at circa 80 instead of Beethoven's 108 - compare with Furtwängler's 66, Walter and Bernstein's 68-9 and Toscanini's 73), develops to a grandiose climax (mighty brass), and the "presto" coda should be played in hospitals: it would lift a paralytic out of his wheelchair.

Scherchen's 8th is one of the most incredible performances I've ever heard, especially in the outer movements, taken at breathtaking speeds and with furious, even raging energy, and filled with a sparkling, explosive exuberance. I've never heard quite anything like it, certainly not before 1954, and not since either, and it is uplifting. Toscanini (in his "official", 1952 recording) sounds civilized and mellow in comparison - contrary to his reputation his tempos are here in fact well within established tradition: just compare his 9:34 to Scherchen's 8:20 in the first movement (yes, Scherchen DOES take the repeat) and their respective 7:27 and 6:22 in the finale. Even Norrington here sounds more relaxed, taking these outer movements in 8:42 and 7:00. René Leibowitz's illuminating cycle from 1961 with modern orchestra (the superlative RPO) was always taken at brisk tempos and his are versions I always come back to as yardsticks ([[ASIN:B000003GDJ Beethoven: Symphonies 6 & 8]]). There is something of Scherchen's exuberance and explosiveness - but it is not quite as radical and furious.

Yes, I can associate this kind of headlong fury with Beethoven, much more than the mellower approaches favored by a certain tradition, whatever the latter's musical merits may be. And note that, however suffocating those tempos may seem, they remain significantly UNDER Beethoven's jawdropping metronome marks: Scherchen is at 56-57 (dotted half-notes/mn) in the first movement to Beethoven's 66, and at 80 to Beethoven's 84 in the finale - that's close enough. The allegretto scherzando marches at a brisk tempo - close enough again to Beethoven's metronome mark although slightly under - and with marvellous vigor. The Tempo di Menuetto has great sweep and robust accenting, although the trumpets don't have the infectious military glare that Bernstein (his first recording, with New York) or Norrington bring to it. The RPO is a winner throughout, playing with great beef.

Given Scherchen's very strict approach to Beethoven's metronome, one is surprised to find instances where he doesn't do so, and conspicuously strays from them. Although recorded at the same time as the Eighth, his First Symphony is very classical and middle-of-the-road. His tempos are unhurried, always slower than Beethoven's metronome marks, and hence I find that his reading lacks the element of dynamism and exuberance that makes the interpretations featured here so unique, illuminating and ultimately indispensable. It is just a good, middle-of-the-road First that doesn't stand out in any way and whose distant mono sound makes it a non runner. In fact I don't understand how the same recording sessions could have yielded such a unique 8th and such a bland 1st. Likewise in the scherzo from the 6th (the Merry Gathering). Scherchen's opening tempo is similar to Walter's, circa 88 dotted half-notes a minute, and a far cry from Beethoven's zipping 108, while his central allegro is a precipitous 147 quarter notes, to Beethoven's 132. Walter here is also faster (138) but he has the orchestra play with uplifting vigor; Scherchen's Vienna Opera Orchestra here sounds ragged and undisciplined, and this is the least satisfying movement in his Pastorale. Surprisingly, his ensuing storm is also disappointing: not so much a matter of tempo (he is sligthly faster than Beethoven's, which is fine in principle, as it lends it greater urgency) as of the lack of snap and explosiveness of his brass, and it comes nowhere near the terrifying violence of Leibowitz. But his finale flows nicely, bang at Beethoven's tempo (and, inexplicably, his brass truly ring again), lending it a great sense of exultant joy, and Scherchen never lets it sag into a gently lulling sway that the ternary rhythms can so easily and surrepticiously bring about.

Anyway, at Scherchen's most radical, everybody, and especially Beethoven-lovers raised on the traditions of Bruno Walter and Furtwängler, no doubt will be shocked, and might even resent it. But, like it or not (and believe it or not), this is not just Scherchen's Beethoven: it is Beethoven's Beethoven. I refer you to my review of Leibowitz' Pastorale and Symphony No. 8 (link above) where, based on Rudolf Kolisch's seminal essay on "tempo and character in the music of Beethoven" (itself based on Beethoven's own writings), I point out the importance that Beethoven ascribed to of a strict observance of his metronome tempos.

"I consider the invention of the metronome a welcome means of assuring that the performance of my compositions everywhere will be in the tempi that I conceived, which to my regret have so often been misunderstood."

Indeed they have, and it didn't stop with the invention of the metronome. Other approaches are perfectly valid and illuminating, and nobody would want to be without Furtwängler's or Klemperer's or Barbirolli's Beethoven. The composer's view is only the first view, not the last and not the ultimate. Still, any serious Beethovenian owes it to himself no listen to Scherchen - not just casually listen and contemptuously dismiss it: listen intently, return regularly to it, let it sink in and break through the patina of your old listening habits (patina: painting conservators call it "dirt"), and reach back to what is, arguably, Beethoven's Beethoven.
user_history.review_title: Scherchen's Beethoven won't be most people's Beethoven - yet this is, in all likelihood, Beethoven's Beethoven

product_meta.title: Goehr: Romanza for Cello & Orchestra/Symphony in One Movement
description: 1. Romanza for Cello and Orchestra, Op. 242. Symphony in One Movement.
product_meta.store: Alexander Goehr (b. 1932)  (Composer),     Daniel Barenboim  (Conductor),     Edward Downes  (Conductor),     Jacqueline du Pre  (Performer),     New Philharmonia  (Orchestra)    &                   2                  more   Format: Audio CD

user_history.review_text:
The exceptional value of this recording compels the music lover to disregard, in Alexander Goehr's Romanza, the annoyance of the constant static that mars the sonic quality of what is visibly an air-check off the radio, that otherwise comes in sound that is clear and vivid enough. Goehr composed his Romanza for and dedicated it to Jacqueline du Pré, who premiered it with her recently-wed husband Daniel Barenboim at the Brighton Festival, in April 1968. Here the product info claims that the performance was given in October 1968 at the royal Festival Hall in London, and I have no way to check.

"Romanza": the title is deceptive if that it lets you expect a short, minor, romantic work. It is 25 minutes long and Romanza is an important and magnificent, fully-fledged Cello Concerto, displaying all the hallmarks of Goehr's compositional style: mostly brooding and lyrical in Goehr's own, atonal way - but maybe even more lyrical and melodious than usually with Goehr, thanks perhaps to the instrument and the performer for whom it was meant, although I just heard Goehr's Violin Concerto from 1962 and it is also very lyrical, see my review of [[ASIN:B00061S0BE British Composers: Hamilton, Goehr]] - with some passages of great mystery and sensuousness, interrupted by explosive outbursts to the point of brutality, freely rapsodic but with a sense of logical unfolding that one perceives even if one doesn't analyze it, certainly not "easy-listening" but full of wonderful touches of compositional imagination. The repertoire is unique for du Pré (other than Priaulx Rainier's Cello Concert, which she performed once and hated, I'm not aware that she played and even less recorded any other piece of contemporary music). This should be a must for any du Pré admirer - even if they admire her more for Elgar and Brahms than for hear feats in contemporary music.

The Symphony dates from two years later and we get here the premiere performance from May 1970 by Edward Downes conducting the same New Philharmonia at the same Royal Festival Hall, London, in fine sound (more about that anon). There is nothing "lyrical" or "melodious" here; as in the Romanza, there are moments of broodingness - the beginning strikingly features a cello solo cantilena after a short orchestral intro, and if you are not listening attentively you might think you are in the Romanza's next movement - but you soon realize that this is only the pent-up, menacing vortex of energy that will rise in the course of the symphony's half-hour, pile up, erupt and lead to a climax (around 24:30) of brutal violence, for which I can see only Varèse's Amériques as a forerunner. The composition is definitely not for all ears, but it is impressive, awesome, and quite unique.

These two works have been granted studio recordings ([[ASIN:B00000E97J Metamorphosis / Dance / Romanza for Cello & Orchestra]] and [[ASIN:B00000DD75 Piano Cto Op 33 / Symphony in One Movement Op 29]]); given the sonic problems of Romanza, the Unicorn disc must be given preference. On the other hand, it is the live Intaglio recording that has, and by a wide margin, the most vivid sound, presence and impact over its competitor; in fact, the sonics of the NMC disc are so dulled (and the interpretation as well) that you could easily miss that the Symphony is the powerful masterpiece that it is. So the Intaglio disc remains indispensable, as a document for Romanza and as a first choice for the Symphony. I am usually not too well disposed towards the kind of bootleg label as Intagl'io, but hey, who else has brought these invaluable recordings to the public? So: thank you.
user_history.review_title: flawed sonics in Romanza, but invaluable recordings nonetheless

product_meta.title: Lumiere, Musique Des Monasteres En Aquitaine Sequentia
product_meta.store: Sequentia Men's Ensemble  (Artist)    Format: Audio CD

user_history.review_text:
Three years after “[[ASIN:B000001TXQ Dante and the Troubadours]]”, recorded in December 1993, which explored the art of the 12 century secular musician-poets from Aquitaine, Benjamin Bagby and Barbara Thornton’s precious Sequentia offer interpretations of manuscripts from 12th century Aquitanian monasteries now held at the French Bibliothèque Nationale de France and the British Library. “With a profusion of thriving spiritual communities, both male and female, [Aquitaine] provided the natural cradle for nurturing and innovating tradition in ways that were to ultimately form the very essence of Western musical thinking and poetics”

“Interpretations” indeed. As Thornton and Bagby say in the liner notes, “in all the polyphonic sources, the musical notation is reasonably clear and set on a staff with clefs, but uses symbols which are devoid of inherent rhythmic significance. This fact is reflected in our performances, in which the texts themselves serve as rhythmic focal-points and rhetorical guides. The notation of the monophonic songs, in certain sources, is found written without a staff or c-clef, making a reconstruction necessary”.

Well, we’ll never know if this is really how this music was performed in 12th century Aquitaine – but it doesn’t matter much. Ultimately, what counts is not historical accuracy (even supposing this accuracy could be firmly established), but the musical pleasure derived by the listener. And once again Sequentia sends you in another world of sublime, contemplative beauty.

Texts are about Mary and the birth of Jesus, and track 4 about Saint Nicholas. Besides a few monophonic settings, the songs offer examples of early polyphony, two-part (although Sequentia’s rendition makes Lux Refulget, the one that opens the disc, sound like a three-part setting).

The recital offers a lot of variety within its apparent “monotony”. It alternates nicely between female and male voices, and intersperses a few instrumental interludes (tracks 5, 8) and a postlude (20) as they would, might, or could have been played in the monasteries (“especially in a celebratory, non-liturgical context”). Some of the polyphonic songs are also underpinned by medieval fiddle and/or rebec (11 male, 18 female). Even in the few monodies (14, 18), Sequentia vary by introducing a solo-chorus responsorial (14) or instrumental underpinning (18).

Some of the polyphonies are of the simplest kind (tracks 3, 16, 19), with a bass pedal (I think those were originally known as the “tenor” part, holding – “tenir” – the note) or “vocal drone” as the liner notes call them, usually sung here by choir, over which the upper voice (usually solo, but partly chorus in 19) unfolds its melismatic garlands. All are sung here by men.

But the polyphony can be more complex. Track 2, “Verbum patris humanatur” offers the kind of dogged two-part polyphony for men’s voice reminiscent of Leonin and Perotin – underlined by the recurring repeat of the vowels “O-O” and the jubilant refrain “eya nova gaudia” (“hurrah, such are the good news”).But most songs present the free and florid interlacing of two voices, female (tracks 4, 7, 9, 10, 17) or male (6, 11, 13, 15), in which again Sequentia provides much variety by alternating solo and choir. The disc opens with such a two-part female polyphony in which the voices gambol and interlace sensuously in the stratosphere, as an adumbration of eternal bliss. In the poem “Virga lesse floruit” (“the branch of Jesse flowered, flowering it grew radiant”, track 12), the liner notes refer to “a very structured poem [which] serves as a trellis for the intertwining ‘viney’ voices as they curve and curl and ornament around meaning” and that describes it perfectly. If you listen carefully to track 15, it is fascinating how some specific harmonies sung by the two men seem to “buzz”.

A contemplative quality emerges from the music, with time flowing very slowly.

Deutsche Harmonia Mundi published two editions of this disc, the English edition, DHM 05472 77370 2, "[[ASIN:B0013AWTFU Shining Light--Music from the Aquitanian Monasteries]]" and this one, the French edition, DHM 05472 77662, Liner notes come only in French on the latter, they are in English, German and French in the former, but paper quality is (consequently?) better (thicker) in the French edition. Texts of poems and translations provided (in the three languages in both editions).
user_history.review_title: Time flowing very slowly - French edition

user_history.review_text:
First, the TT of 47 minutes all but rules out this disc. The recordings date from 1979 (Bartok, Janos Ferencsik conducting - it is a live recording, as revealed by very occasional coughs and various stage noises, and the final applause) and 1980 (Berg - studio, Vaclav Neumann at the baton) and were originally published in the ending days of the LP - but this is LP duration, and the CD reissue should have been augmented. The interpretations would have to be really exceptional to warrant purchase, when those works are available in so many other and great recordings.

They aren't.

Since Isaac Stern and Eugene Ormandy's 1961 premiere recording of the newly discovered youtfhful concerto of Bartok ([[ASIN:B000002A8I A Life In Music: Isaac Stern, Volume 9]], it was first performed in 1958 in Basle, by Hanz-Heinz Schneeberger and conductor and wealthy patron of music Paul Sacher), there have been a number of very successful recordings that have underlined the ecstatic, time-suspended quality of the first movement, from David Oistrakh ([[ASIN:B0000713AB Szymanowski Violin Concerto No 1; Bartok Violin Concerto No. 1 ; Hindemith: Violin Concerto (Urania)]]) to Midori ([[ASIN:B00000270Y Bartok - Violin Concertos No.1 & No.2 / Midori, Berlin Phil., Mehta]]) and Kremer ([[ASIN:B001AVZN3W Bartok: Concertos]]). But at 10:23 minutes, Suk is the slowest of them all (other than Stern's premiere recording, everybody is under 10 minutes), and with his pulse by the note rather than by the beat, which makes you loose entirely the lilt of Bartok's 6/8 time signature, I feel that the Czech fiddler has overstepped the line between ecstasy and sluggish boredom. His beauty of tone also works against him: stressing the elegiac, he remains somewhat placid and lacks the throbbing bow tension of Oistrakh and Stern. His second movement is better, but you need only to turn to Stern to realize what the soloist and orchestra's greater muscularity and hair of extra drive, added to the Philadelphia's better sonics - with Ferencsik, the violin tuttis are so distant that they deprive the lush, romantic climaxes of any impact - and Stern's fatter tone bring to the music. Again, while hearing Suk play this un-typical, Strauss-indebted music, a sense of boredom insinuates itself, which is dispelled hearing Stern.

In the LP days, when recordings of Berg's Violin Concerto were a really rare commodity (before 1970 you didn't need a third hand to count them), Suk made a really exceptional recording in 1965, one that led the field (the merits of Stern-Bernstein [[ASIN:B0000026EP Berg: Kammerkonzert]], Ferras-Prêtre [[ASIN:B00005RFTE Les Introuvables de Christian Ferras [Box Set]]], Grumiaux-Markevitch [[ASIN:B00000E3TN Berg / Stravinsky: Violin Concerto - Grumiaux, Markevitch, Bour]] and Menuhin-Boulez [[ASIN:B000FULXH4 Berg: Violin Concerto / Bloch: Violin Concerto - Menuhin Edition]] notwithstanding), with the same orchestra (Czech Philharmonic, a supremely virtuosic group) but under its then music director, Karel Ancerl ([[ASIN:B00006IZPL Ancerl Gold Edition 3: Mendelssohn - Bruch - Berg/Violin Concertos]]). It benefited from the clear and vivid sonics affording great detail and pungency to the orchestra, from Suk's pure and stellar tone and also from his relatively cool and unsentimental approach (there's enough emotion in the notes and one doesn't necessarily need to milk it) - although it was perhaps a little too uninflected and matter of fact in the first movement.

The new recording is very similar in conception, a tad faster and still somewhat uninflected in the first movement, and imperceptibly faster as well in the final chorale. In the intervening years Suk has lost little of his purity of tone. But the sonics are muffled, the orchestral details are dulled and the orchestra doesn't approach the bite and pungent power it had under Ancerl. This would remain a valuable version still today - if not one to put on top of the pile - if Suk hadn't done his earlier recording, but as it is, it doesn't add anything to his previous version, but rather subtracts from it.

A disc better reserved then to the most diehard admirers and collectors of Josef Suk. Music-lovers without this particular agenda will do better with Suk's previous recording of Berg's VC under Ancerl, and will have a number of better options in Bartok, and particularly, in the same general conception, those mentioned in the course of this review.
user_history.review_title: Best reserved to the diehard fans of violinist Josef Suk

target_product.review_text:
This is European Vanguard 08 6107 71, the 1996 reissue on their budget series Everyman of a recital already published in 1993 as 08 2005 71, [[ASIN:B0000254LR Passacaglia E Fuga Bwv 582 (1708) in Do]]. The same Bach recital by Anton Heiller also had a US edition, OVC 2005, [[ASIN:B0000023A7 Bach: Organ Works]]. The history of Vanguard CD reissues is a complicated affair and not the subject of this review, but in the 1990s Vanguard's founder Seymour Solomon had (through his company Omega Records) the distribution rights of the Vanguard classical catalog in America, while a Dutch company, Arcade, had them for Europe.

Reviewers of the US edition have complained about the botched sound of OVC 2005, and have forwarded instead to the later SACD edition, ATM-SC 1554, [[ASIN:B0002MPQQY Organ Works]], praising its great sonics. I'm not putting in doubt what they heard on OVC 2005. But I thought it was a real bummer the SACD edition came shorn of Toccata & Fugue BWV 565 and Fantasia and Fugue BWV 542: 20 minutes of music and not the most insignificant either. So I took my chances and bought the European edition, 08 2005 71.

I do not hear there what the reviewers of OVC 2005 are talking about. Yes, heard, very carefully, on headphones, there is a minuscule, one-second dropout in track 2 (Fantasia & Fugue BWV 542) at 0:21, and a vague patch of flutter around 9:19 to say, 9:34, and in track 5 (Passagaclia and Fugue BWV 582), there are three seconds of distinct dropout from 2:45 to 2:48. Other than that and small tape hiss in the softer passages, it sounds simply grandiose. Frankly, 3 or 10 seconds of minuscule sonic glitches weigh nothing in balance with the sonic splendor of that recording and transfer, and the addition of BWV 565 and BWV 542. I also bought the SACD reissue. Heard on a normal, non SACD system, it gains little if anything sonically, while it loses those two major works. With what I hear on 08 2005 71, I really need nothing more sonically.

I don't have this Everyman reissue, but I assume that it uses exactly the same transfer as 08 2005 71 - and, at the time of writing, it sells much cheaper. I don't know what may have been the problem with the American edition, OVC 2005. Was it specific to the American transfers (but I always thought Omega/US and Arcade/Europe used the same) or maybe the CD "pressings" (I'm not sure CDs are "pressed", but you see what I mean), or only to some of the CDs that came out of the US production line? Anyway, if you don't want to take any chances, go for the European edition.

Just for the record, this Heiller-Bach recital was first reissued on CD in the late 1980s, when the rights to the Vanguard catalog were owned by the Welk Music Group, on Vanguard VCD 72014, [[ASIN:B0028FZWT4 Great Bach Organ Works]], with a French release in 1990 by Carrère Vanguard 92523. Comment under the American release complains, but not very specifically, about the poor sound. The program was complemented by two Choral-Preludes not elsewhere reissued to the best of my knowledge, BWV 730 & 731.

product_meta.title: Lombardo Country - Guy Lombardo and His Royal Canadians

user_history.review_text:
Guy Lombardo and the Royal Canadians, LOMBARDO COUNTRY, Capitol T/ST 2777. June, 1967

My copy is the mono.

Lombardo fans at the time (he was a '20s-early '30s icon) got a new album, the Lombardo sound "sweet" big band white alto saxes, restrained brass, steady clock-like drum kit, no hot swing white-hot solos, just steady, predictable dance music.

...with 1960-65 Nashville Sound country songs. Er, strange, strange, strange, if you're a C&W fan like me. Strange....

Track list:
side one--
Anytime (the crooner Eddy Arnold song. Or 1953 Eddie Fisher, if you lean that way.)
He'll Have to Go (the crooner Jim Reeves song. Opens with muted trumpets. Oh, ...!)
Invisible Tears (Sonny James on Capitol)
Your Cheatin' Heart (a Hank Williams weeper as an instrumental...with Lombardo alto saxes....)
Cool Water (Kenny Gardner and the Lombardo Trio stand in for the Sons of the Pioneers)
Wabash Cannon Ball (what would Roy Acuff think???)
side two--
You Are My Sunshine (Governor Jimmie Davis's Great Depression oldie)
Tennessee Waltz (the Pee Wee King or Patti Page hit)
Under Your Spell Again (BUCK OWENS!?!)
Slipping Around (Floyd Tillman)
San Antonio Rose (Bob Wills)

For the most part, the songs work, but sound strange...if you're a country music fan of the old stuff. The Lombardo Great Depression sweet dance band take on "He'll Have to Go" works on that song, but then I really don't care for the Jim Reeves' snore factor on his 1958+ style. Best fits are "Any Time," which sounds like it should date from the early '30s, and the early '30s Jimmie Davis "You Are My Sunshine" standard. Worst don't-fit is "Your Cheatin' Heart," which just does NOT transfer to background ballroom speakeasy dance sound. And Bakersfield Buck Owens' "Under Your Spell Again" working class honky-tonker--UGH!

Kenny Gardner vocals on "Any Time," "Invisible Tears," "Cool Water," "You Are My Sunshine," "Under Your Spell Again." "Wabash Cannon Ball" gets a vocal from Cliff Grass.

One other Lombardo song choice "OOPS!!!" album runs the gauntlet with the later '60s pop (rock-lite) song era, and you gotta look it up if you like DOES NOT FIT: Guy Lombardo, THE NEW SOUNDS, Capitol ST 128 (early 1969). It has an excruciating funny take on Simon & Garfunkel's "Mrs. Robinson," as well was versions of "Honey" (Bobby Goldsboro), "Folsom Prison Blues" (yeah, right, Johnny Cash as a Volstead Act dance tune!), "Scarborough Fair/Canticle" (Simon & Garfunkel, again), and the "Harper Valley P.T.A." tell-off song.

Wink Martindale's vocal artistry is unsurpassed in the record industry; his recording career took off in 1959 after appearing in a rock 'n' roll -theme b&w movie, LET'S ROCK (Julius LaRosa, an exploito rock movie like DON'T KNOCK THE ROCK and ROCK, ROCK, ROCK), performing a big beat rocker classic, "All Love Broke Loose," on Dot 15728, from March, 1958. Possessed by a gorgeous voice and unbelievable range, timbre, and emotion, he had a long recording career at Randy Woods' Dot Records, putting out twenty-one 45RPM singles and five albums. Like Bobby Darin's growth from teen records to adult-flavored pop, Wink's next release was aimed at the broader pop market. His reading of "Deck of Cards" on Dot 15968 45 single (his second release on the label) ran up to #4 on the Cash Box Pop Singles chart; Dot rushed out this album, DECK OF CARDS, Dot DLP 3245 (mono)/DLP 25245 (stereo; roughly February/March, 1960.) to exploit his single's success.

Song selection:
side one--
Deck of Cards/Melody of Love/Steal Away/Just a Closer Walk with Thee/The Shifting Whispering Sands
side two--
Peace in the Valley/Trees/Beyond the Sunset/Little Boy Blue/Moon River

Note: "Moon River" on side two is NOT the Andy Williams' version.

As with other late '50s/early '60s popular albums, the mono versions far outsold the stereo copies (mono list price $3.98; stereo copies were premium priced at $4.98 list; additionally, it took record buyers some years to upgrade their hi-fi sets to play stereo records). My copy is the mono version and I've yet to score the more elusive stereo copy. Dot's vinyl Lps were among the best quality on vinyl Lp, and Dot made great sounding true stereo early recordings instead of resorting to rechanneling mono catalog in the early '60s.

Wink's all-around musical talents include that as a songwriter, placing one of two sides on Al Martino's April, 1963, Capitol 5183 single, "A Year Ago Tonight," which was also an Lp cut on Martino's Capitol T/ST 2107 Lp from early 1964, I LOVE YOU MORE AND MORE EVERYDAY/TEARS & ROSES.

Should you wish to check out Wink's recording history on Lp, here's a list of his Lps--

DECK OF CARDS, Dot DLP 3245/DLP 25245 (early 1960)
BIBLE STORY, Dot DLP 3293/25293
BIG BAD JOHN, Dot DLP 3403/25403
MY TRUE LOVE, Dot DLP 3571/25571
GIDDYUP GO, Dot DLP 3696/25696 (July, 1966)
--Note: any Hamilton Lps were Dot's half-price budget bin repackages of older catalog, until Dot leased out the masters to the dreadful Pickwick Records at the end of the '60s.

user_history.review_text:
Pat Boone SINGS WINNERS OF THE READER'S DIGEST POLL, Dot DLP 3667 mono/DLP 25667 stereo. This vinyl Lp dates about October, 1965.

This Lp is probably the nadir of Boone's album sales; it's especially difficult to locate a copy, and worse (rarer) in stereo. Boone attempted to change his commercial style in early 1963, softening his choices and themes with more sedate middle-of-the-road easy listening albums, beginning with his February, 1963 Lp, DAYS OF WINE AND ROSES AND OTHER GREAT MOVIE THEMES, Dot DLP 3504/25504, and this Lp marks the end of that trail in his career.

Track list:
side one--

side two--
Tea for Two
All The Things You Are
I Left My Heart in San Francisco
We Gaze on Tomorrow
As Time Goes By
Ol' Man River

Produced by Randy Wood. Arranged by Pete King; the orchestra is big and lush, emphasizing a large string section, harps, flutes, woodwinds, muted piano, muted horns. Biggest surprise on the Lp is his jazzy Big Band uptempo version of "Ol' Man River," the best track on the Lp. At the time of this release, the Billboard Top 150 Lp chart acts were the Beatles' HELP, Sonny & Cher, soundtracks THE SOUND OF MUSIC, MY FAIR LADY, and MARY POPPINS, Ramsey Lewis THE IN CROWD, and Barbra Streisand's MY NAME IS BARBRA (per the 10/30/65 chart), so Boone's sedate album here is right in the bullseye ring for commercial album styles at the time.

"We Gaze On Tomorrow" shows songwriting credit to "Boone/King"; however, the tune/music is the "Greensleeves" old chestnut with new lyrics.

Three and a half stars. Stereo copies on this can be almost impossible.

product_meta.title: On Tour Through Motortown
description: LP - The New Christy Minstrels On Tour Through Motortown 1968 CS 9616 Columbia Record Label; Stereo version

target_product.review_text:
The idea of this album is off the meter. -- April, 1968

You might imagine, in the aftermath of the Beatles' SGT. PEPPER Lp the year before, if Pat Boone ...or Lawrence Welk... had sponsored his version of the Mamas & the Papas, then whitewashed Motown soul. Stylistically, this album more than suggests the Mike Curb Congregation's WALT DISNEY'S GREATEST HITS a few years later. Smiley-happy, white vacant amusement park interchangable employees happily singing more-than-vanilla versions of Motown catalog.

It's a short package--10 songs, even for a period Lp. Normally Columbia pop albums had 11 tracks when this package issued, which suggests that this album was shorted one song, mostly likely to cut down on the mechanical royalty payments due for Barry Gordy's song catalog. Track list:

Side one--
Dancing in the Streets/Where Did Our Love Go/Reach Out (I'll Be There)/Stop in the Name of Love/Ain't Gonna Waste My Time
Side two--
Shotgun/Ain't No Mountain High Enough/My Girl/A Place in the Sun/Just Look at Her Now

"Where Did Our Love Go," "Stop in the Name of Love," and "A Place in the Sun" are treated as dreamy slow ballads, a la what the Doodletown Pipers did to the Beatles' "A Hard Day's Night," and the Christies' own execreble slow version of "I Want to Hold Your Hand" on their NEW KICK album a little before. The male group vocals on "My Girl" wreaks of earnestness. "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" is also slowed down, and the lead male vocal just calls out a vocal presence resembling Conway Twitty, if he'd crooned lounge. The album ends with a comic reading (ugh) version of "Just Look At Her Now," complete with "wah-wah-wah..." alto sax and muted trumpet aping laughing, and guitar with a "wah-wah" pedal. Overall, the band and backing on this set sounds like the house band for an early '70s variety/music TV show like those by Tony Orlando & Dawn, Jim Nabors, etc...--not quite right funky bass and rock guitar, too loud horn section over-weighed by trumpets blasting away, add the occasional harpsicord, orchestra string section, just oozing "This is SHOW BUSINESS!!!"

From the late '60s, this is one of three albums Columbia and affiliated acts don't seem to want remembered/reissued: The Brothers Four, THE LENNON-MCCARTNEY SONGBOOK, and Tony Bennett, SINGS THE GREAT HITS OF TODAY.

Kitsch recommended!

product_meta.store: Bones and Tones  (Artist)    Format: Audio CD

user_history.review_text:
One review reads 'A marimba, a vibraphone, a stand-up bass, percussion and a little kora. A little bit of American jazz, a dash of Caribbean and a side of African folk music, but not quite like any of the three. How sweet the sound.

That's the kind of sound coming from this one-of-kind quartet Tones And Bones. A crew heavily steeped in knowledge about percussion type instruments T and B came together for the specific purpose for performing at the Long Beach Jazz Festival, and decided to take the collaboration further, into the studio. After listening to the results, I would add, "thankfully so." Comprising of Abdou Mboup (vocals, kora and percussion), Jaribu Shahid (bass and percussion), Lloyd Haber (marimba, bells and percussion) and favorite around here, Warren Smith (vibraphone and percussion), the quartet pooled together their talents to interpret fresh compositions from Haber and Smith to craft music that's exotic, and more full of tonality than you might think given the setup.

It's probably a little more tonal than you might think it'd be given the credentials of Smith and Haber(Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry, etc.), but each of them give us tunes that are quite harmonious. Smith's "228" has a warm sound in spite of the bank of percussion roaring in at various spots before disappearing again. That can be attributed to Smith's vibes that are voluminous and swinging like Milt Jackson. Haber's "Song For The Old Ones" as it's a well written composition is another highlight; he takes the lead on this one with Smith providing the dulcet shadings behind him.

Mboup sings in his native West African tongue for the opener ("Breathing Water" and the closer "In The Valley of Dreams." On both of those songs, Mboup also plays his 21 string lute instrument, the kora. The enchanting, soothing sound of the kora fit so well with the marimba and vibraphone, it's kind of a shame it wasn't used more throughout the album. As a percussionist, Mboup and the others modulates their rhythms well, never overwhelming Haber and Smith. He and Shahid work together to construct smart grooves that bolster the songs ("Dance For Suwoo" and "MR7" are good examples of that), and not turn them into runaway rhythm fests.'

product_meta.title: Bliss - Music for Reiki & Healing Therapy

user_history.review_text:
"Reiki (霊気) is a form of alternative medicine developed in 1922 by Mikao Usui. Since originating in Japan, reiki has been adapted into varying cultural traditions.." It reportedly began being taught in India around 1992.

This CD has 14 tracks, unnamed, averaging 4-5 minutes each. The musical focus is 2 (overdubbed) flute lines, with slight musical setting of keyboard and acoustic guitar. The music is all in free rhythm, and there is no drum or meter. One track flows into the next, and sometimes there is a different tonal center ('supporting chord').

The chief musician is Rakesh Chaurasia, the award-winning nephew of Hariprasad Chaurasia, the best and most famous bansuri player of this era.

The album could be simply new-age aural pablum; it's saved from that ignoble fate by the talent of Rakesh. Find his many other recordings to hear his great talent and what he's actually capable of.

It's not "music for listening" nor is it intended to be. It's marketed as music to be played in reiki healing; I'm guessing it will serve that purpose well. It would also work well at a low volume for going to sleep, adult or infant. It's purposefully non-exciting and does not draw attention to itself. It serves well as background music for various purposes.

user_history.review_text:
Cracker Barrel's 500 stores now have listening stations equipped with headphones where you can hear selections from their catalog of heritage albums that span bluegrass to Celtic, country to Cajun, and Native American to traditional jazz. Launched in collaboration with the National Council for the Traditional Arts, the label celebrates regionally-inspired traditional music.

In 2002, East Tennessee country singer Linda Lay put out an especially pleasant package of classic country favorites called "Linda's Mercantile Store" (CB-101). Successful shows and rave reviews in support of that album led to the trio of Linda and David Lay, along with David McLaughlin, to stay together as a band called Springfield Exit. Guests include Rickie Simpkins (fiddle) and Ricky Davis (pedal steel).

Raised in Bristol, Virginia, Linda Lay was singing on stage with her father and uncles by the time she was only six. She and her husband used to perform with the band, Appalachian Trail, and they now have a vegetable farm and country store in the Goshen Valley of Tennessee. She sings and plays acoustic bass.
David Lay is a talented harmony singer and solid rhythm guitar player. From east Tennessee, he has traveled extensively and has been a featured guitarist with the Masters of the Steel String Guitar.
A full-time musician since 1978, David McLaughlin was a founding member of The Johnson Mountain Boys, a group twice nominated for a Grammy Award. He has played the Grand Ole Opry, the White House, Carnegie Hall, and on TNN. In the mid-1990s, he was with the country and folk duo, Crowe & McLaughlin. McLaughlin plays several instruments and sings harmony with Springfield Exit.

Springfield Exit's instrumental prowess, singing, and song selection make for a pleasant experience.
"Miss Linda" has a magnetic voice, and she has an affinity for singing stories about life drawn from the pens of Tom T. and Dixie Hall, Dolly Parton, Hazel Dickens, Don Williams, Greg Brown, Dale Ann Bradley and Vicki Simmons, and others. Springfield Exit's country cookin' primarily simmers on a burner of slower to moderate tempos with toe-tapping rhythms. While certainly not bluegrass in its truest sense, the band has a relaxed and comfortable commercial sound with classic country sensibilities. Linda sings powerfully and with good vocal control. Songs are nicely arranged and are tastefully delivered. Springfield Exit will bring many hours of listening enjoyment to fans of acoustic country music with light percussion and pedal steel. (Joe Ross, California Bluegrass Association reviewer)

user_history.review_text:
The pandemic didn’t slow down Slide Attack, a quintet with trombonists Alan Goidel and Howard Levy, Hiroshi Yamazaki (piano), Michael Goetz (bass) and Chuck Zeuren (drums). During 2020, they masked up and socially distanced during rehearsals and recording sessions. Slide Attack blends elements of vintage and modern jazz as they play fast and fluidly through nine original compositions. Opening with Yamazaki’s “Spring Roll,” the band makes an emphatic statement with propulsive solos. In Goidel’s swinging “Road Trip,” the journey is happy, joyous and carefree as Levy incorporates some rapid-paced growls and slurs to approximate scat-like vocal effects. His inspiration for the up-tempo, bebopping “Owens” came from Gershwin’s “I Got Rhythm” and allows both trombonists to get imaginative just as they also do on “Bluedemic,” a composition that channels Charlie Parker.

Levy’s “Clauditti” has a Brazilian samba groove, while the funky forward momentum of “Struttin’” is driven by Zeuren’s percussion. The two trombonists are creative, and their artistic expression really shines on the slower, lyrical pieces like “Look Within,” “A Walk in the Park” and “Early Morning.” Goidel and Levy are straight-forward, unpretentious players who emphasize sensibility over flamboyance. Together, the two-trombone quintet features pliable musicians who work well together. They also show how that instrument can be centerstage and plugged into more than just nostalgic traditional arrangements. The music reminds me of some of the material that trombonist Kai Winding produced with other masters of the instrument, J. J. Johnson and Curtis Fuller. Now, I’m wondering if Slide Attack’s next Road Trip might even bring along a third or fourth trombonist for even more adventure and excitement. (Joe Ross, Roots Music Report)
user_history.review_title: Straight-forward, unpretentious players who emphasize sensibility over flamboyance

user_history.review_text: Based in Baltimore, guitarist Ahmed Warshanna holds a degree in Jazz Studies, and his debut album Ishta demonstrates his unique compositional and arranging skills informed by a passion for combining element of both the East and West into his music. The five tracks, each ranging from 7-10 minutes in length, create aural experiences that range from plaintive (“Azra’”) to exhilarating (“Intisar”). The first two tracks, Warshanna’s arrangements of classics by Egyptian singer Umm Kulthum, set the stage with intrigue, using Middle Eastern scales with resonant chords and rhythmic percussive sounds. Arranged for septet, the guitarist’s music also showcases the musicianship of Hart Guonjian-Pettit (trumpet), Dominic Ellis (tenor), Daniel Sperlein (trombone), Joshua Miller (piano), Thomas Owens (bass) and Charlie Seda (drums). Kulthum was known to sing her songs at length and in depth, and Warshanna takes a similar approach with his septet’s instruments. Ishta has plenty of atmospheric instrumental dynamics, but perhaps some vocals and ud could’ve been used to make them even more mysterious. Warshanna’s music may be rooted in the organic Egyptian earth, but it also conveys his uncompromising, honest desire to make a transcendent contemporary statement. The album is a tribute to Ahmed’s mother who passed away in 2021. She brought music into his life, and he acknowledges that this music was inspired by her and that she’ll live on through his music. (Joe Ross, Roots Music Report)

user_history.review_text:
Peaking at #15 on The Roots Music Report's Top 50 World Album Chart back in January, 2022, it was a delight to hear Stefano Saletti & Banda Ikona sing their stories of the “tenacious Mediterranean and its ancient, resilient people” accompanied by a variety of string, wind and percussion instruments. Multi-instrumentalist Stefano Saletti plays bouzouki, oud, saz, guitar, tzouras, gambrì, cavaquinho, piano, bodhran, darbouka, tammorra and marranzano. Other band members layer clarinet, sax, bass and various drums into the mix, while guests color arrangements with occasional violin, organetto, ney, daf, ciaramella, cello, percussion and added vocals. At track 3, “Boulegar” even enlists the Baobab ensemble for a full choir of vocalizing.

Opening the set with “Anima de Moundo,” the vocals of Barbara Eramo and Yasemin Sannino sweetly converse with Alessandro D'Alessandro’s organetto and Renato Vecchio’s ciaramella (Italian bagpipes). Another track receiving good airplay is the reflective, slower-tempo’ed ballad, “Canterrante’ that sensuously features Lucilla Galeazzi’s vocals, Riccardo Tesi’s organetto, and Giovanna Famulari’s cello. The title track, “Mediterraneo Ostinato” speaks of people who are stubborn, combative, obstinate and refuse to give up. It may have some socio-political meaning to address new forms of injustice, marginalization and a growing gap between the wealthy and poor.

While hints of traditional music enter the set (“Nare Nare” and “Se Fossi Foco”), the majority is contemporary acoustic world music, written by Saletti, with folk, ethnic and current perspectives. It seems that Mediterraneo Ostinato is a manifesto of a possible new “Mediterranean Power” that draws from an artistic culture of the past to present a hopeful, optimistic, connected future full of heart and soul.

The unique lyrics are sung in Sabir, an ancient Mediterranean language revived in Saletti’s original compositions inspired by the region’s literature and poetry. It was a language used by sailors, pirates, fishermen, merchants and ship-owners to communicate with one another, availing itself of terms from Spanish, Italian, French and Arabic. A project to unite the peoples of the Mediterranean, its soothing feel might also have a calming effect on the world at large, something that is much needed at this time in our global history.

As the album closes with “Maréia” (featuring only bouzouki and cello) and then“Cantar,” we feel somewhat like ancient travelers ourselves, ever discovering links to the past, encountering fresh insights, and exploring new environments. Stefano Saletti and Banda Ikona will no doubt continue their performing, recording and touring to take their musical statements about the need for collaboration and unification to an even larger global audience. (Joe Ross, Roots Music Report)
user_history.review_title: Stories of the “tenacious Mediterranean & its ancient, resilient people”

user_history.review_text:
Playing Time - 44:52 -- SONGS: 1. Business, 2. Rain Check, 3. The Sky Is Falling, 4. Run Away, 5. Get The Lead Out, 6. Left Out, 8. Rocket Ride, 8. White Window, 9. Suddenly, 10. Pessimistic Proposal, 11. One Man Band, 12. Cheap Date, 13. Light, 14. Regret

Singer-songwriter Benjamin Olson describes his music as "pop-sensible Americana folk-rock." He has a few catchy melodies, and he seems sincere in the delivery of his lyrics although a song like "Left Out" challenges his range on the low register. Originally from Wisconsin, Olson started writing songs at age 15, and he had over 100 songs by the time he graduated high school. He eventually found himself Nashville in 2003. While he had played drums and piano (and does so on a couple tracks of "White Window"), his favorite instrument is now the guitar. Others on the album include Rod Lewis (bass, vox), Tim Grogan (drums, percussion, keys, vox), and Howard Buckwold (electric guitar, mandolin).

Olson appears to be reaching out to the Americana market, and his challenge is to create memorable songs.
His music seems more in tune with the Austin scene than perhaps Nashville. His best efforts are "One Man Band," "The Sky is Falling," "Regret," and "3d Rocket Ride." While "Regret" is regretfully a little short (under two minutes), it has a nice acoustic flavoring in comparison to the drum-heavy and throbbing opener, "Business," which has punk or grunge overtones. "Rain Check" starts with a haunting feel then the song's genesis takes us through some dynamics of various tonal and rhythmic colors. The title cut, an instrumental piano piece with eerie synthesizer which appears at track 8, seems a bit out of place sandwiched between the more raucous offerings. However, it does showcase his piano playing in a rather lean, almost demo-like, arrangement. "Suddenly" then establishes a funky groove as it relates a enigmatic recipe. Despite Olson's perseverance and dedication to his craft, the message in "Pessimistic Proposal" could be construed as a rather defeatist attitude when it comes to love-gone-wrong or rejection.

To get his messages further heard and understood, Olson should've included his lyrics in the CD jacket. Stylistically, "White Window" shows that Benjamin Olson shows promise as a budding songwriter. I'd encourage him to listen to some guys like Tom Russell, Jon Randall, Rodney Crowell and Ryan Shupe for a better handle on the alt country genre. I did appreciate his ability to combine blues, rock, punk and funk rhythms into his music. With some good support and a bit of luck, we could be hearing much more about Benjamin Olson in the near future. (Joe Ross)

user_history.review_text:
The hungry yellow flames licking at the damp fall air have begun to recede into a seething crimson that now casts a trance-inducing glow on the windowpanes outside of Zoloto Station. A foreshadowing veil of darkness has dispatched the artists from their cozy bonfire reclines resulting in five sets of footprints in the dew covered grass leading to the back door. Soon, even as the aroma of tobacco and red wine is still dissipating with smouldering ashes into the night, a thick chunky bass and percussion groove from within, ripples the gold tinted glass with a pulsing intensity inspired by elements of funk, dub reggae, trip hop and African legend Fela Kuti. As you begin to release your whole body to the seduction of these rhythmic waves, the folky drone of the tenor guitar, moaning cello, silky violin and mind numbing ebow take turns sending you deeper. Now that you can no longer think, but only feel the embrace of the music, you are carried away by a smooth passionate vocal that shares all of her emotions and holds you close until you have reached your own personal state of ...zoebliss.

What started as a solo recording project by singer/songwriter Brenley MacEachern (vocals, acoustic guitar, tenor guitar) at Adrian Lawryshyn's (bass, guitar, cello & songwriter) studio in Terra Cotta, Ontario (NW of Toronto) in early 1997 quickly developed into a symbiotic creation of zoebliss. On April 13th, after spending thirty of the last fourty-eight hours together recording 'Where are you', Brenley and Adrian knew, without even saying that a partnership was born. Brenley's Folk roots, melodic hooks and provocative lyrics combined with Adrian's funky bass lines, diverse arrangements and passion for rythem allowed the amalgamation of their musical visions to grow into a unique sonic mosaic.

With their band not fully formed at the time, but a desire to continue their recording journey without delay, Brenley and Adrian acquired the talents of several well-known Toronto musicians for their debut CD. Enter Kurt Swinghammer, whose inventive guitar style, sitar, ebow and mini moog accented the zoebliss sound. Andy Stochansky lent his percussive craft to the project (while on hiatus from the Ani DiFranco tour) incorporating kit, djembe, talking drum and dumbek. Sheila Gruner (of Black Cabbage) laid down some beautiful sinewy violin on a number of songs that compliments the complexity of this music.

The experienced trio of Andrew Trigg (percussion), Mike Rockwood (guitar), and John Hall (drums) were brought on as permanent members of zoebliss in the spring of '98. The melding of this quintet of musicians brings to the fore a fresh expressive style that combines magnified originality, musical diversity and outstanding vocals, which the band refers to as "folky trip-hop".

With the release of their debut CD '13april' in June of '98 the band immediately peaked the interest of the record industry. In quick succession, following the release of the CD, the band... Played at the NXNE music festival in Toronto... Was chosen as one of eleven bands from all of the NXNE applicants to appear on Toronto's Edge 102 New Rock Search CD. Received airplay of their first single 'Wicked Ways' on Edge 102 and campus radio and they opened for The Wild Strawberries and K's Choice at the CNE in Toronto. In July, the band travelled to New York City for a showcase at the request of Just Talent ( formally ID Entertainment), a management company who currently handles artists such as Tricky, Bad Religion, Victoria Williams and MeShell N'degeocello. 'Just Talent', who now represents zoebliss in the U.S. promptly acquired some 'demo' capital from MCA in Los Angeles and are currently working towards promoting the band state side. For their part the band is already writing new songs for their next release and has been performing material from '13april' over the last few months on a club tour.

The cohesiveness displayed by this band is certainly not indicative of their short time spent together. It is easy to find yourself enslaved in the melodic passion of zoebliss that allows the mood of the moment to take you over as each artist leaves a little piece of themselves right there on the stage as open and as raw as the penetrating music itself.

user_history.review_text:
The late conductor Karl Bohm (1894-1981) left a vast hoard of studio recordings, radio broadcasts, public concerts, and live operas. The Memories label has gathered a series of concerts, between 1953 and 1957, in which he conducts the Frankfort Radio Symphony.
Except for the Beethoven 4th Symphony, which he also recorded later as part of his 1970 cycle of all 9 Symphonies and featuring the Vienna Philharmonic, he chose 3 works that, as far as I can determine, do not appear in his recorded output. The Mozart 22nd Piano Concerto has Wilhelm Kempff's fine playing; the Beethoven 4th is a bit more driven than the 1970 reading but both are moving performances that strengthen Bohm's already solid credentials as a Beethoven authority. Haydn's lovely Cello Concerto No. 2 in D Major has the late, underrated cellist Enrico Mainardi. Finally, and I confess that this was my main motive in buying this set, the Richard Strauss Symphonia Domestica has an element of volatile rambunctiousness that Bohm conveys fully. I now own about 17 different recordings, all of them having something interesting, and my favorite is Reiner's, which was recorded in November, 1956, just over 1 month before Bohm's concert. Still, I would advise anyone who loves great conducting and collects interesting duplicate recordings of favorite pieces not to miss this set.
user_history.review_title: A pleasurable package of repertoire, most of which Bohm did not record commercially.

user_history.review_text:
I have an exorbitant love for the Brahms 2nd Symphony and his 4th- they win out in my affections by an admittedly slight margin over the 1st and the 3rd, which are however still masterpieces.

My memories of the Second go back to just before I entered 8th grade during the fall of 1964. I heard the first movement for the first time by a semi-professional orchestra at a music camp, their playing being quite good. At the same time, I had a 78 album conducted by Eugene Ormandy and released without the maestro's name being credited on the label. I also heard the Toscanini/NBC Symphony RCA Victor LP and bought the Pierre Monteux/Vienna Philharmonic recording. All 3 were very good renditions of this music.
Mehta's performance is a bit hard-driving yet it has plenty of fire and a ferociously intense pacing with a tiny bit of rubato towards the end of the Finale that accelerates both tempi and phrasing and brings it to a rousing conclusion A sometimes hectic reading but very good on its own terms.
Others in my collection include Bohm, Jochum, Bernstein, Giulini, Klemperer, Monteux, Kempe, Levine, Furtwangler, Schuricht and Barbirolli - all of these at least twice- and 2 more by Ormandy. There are also single performances by Fritz Busch, Fritz Reiner, Dohnanyi, Szell, Dorati, Kubelik, Abbado, Boult, Klemperer, Lee, Rudolf, DePriest, Jarvi, Fricsay, Kertesz, Rodzinski, Stokowski, Hollreiser, Koussevitzky, Maazel, Munch, Keilberth, Pisek, Haitink, Abravanel, Savallisch, Leinsdorf and Van Beinum. And all of them are treasurable in some way.
user_history.review_title: A very powerful, almost volatile performance of Brahms's wonderful  2nd Symphony that warrants consideration.

product_meta.store: サヨナライツカ   Format: Audio CD

user_history.review_text:
One of the more unfortunate things about music scenes that develop a sound is that sometimes one finds a band that manages to break out of the pattern, forge a path, and the band leaves little in the way of recorded legacy or information. This has happened on several occasions with Japan’s math rock scene, which has a few truly original leading lights, but also, if one is honest, some tropes that can become worn. Clean guitars that sound a little too linear for a subgenre that is supposed to be built upon angularity, if not done well, although there is so much great music to be found. Then there are the groups that release one album and that’s it. Consider Muddy World, whose sole release, Finery of the Storm, is a high point in the genre, partly for sounding like no one else. Here, consider Sayonaraitsuka, or however one chooses to transliterate the name into Latin-based characters. The Fragments of Resurrection has many of the core elements one will find on releases from bands like toe and LITE, which sort of define the nation’s take on the genre, yet rather than either linearity in defiance of the concept of math rock, or mere angularity in strict adherence to the form, the band casts about, seeking. Some of the more successful math rock groups in Japan draw on jazz or post-rock, like jizue, JYOCHO or mouse on the keys, but few draw on a kind of RIO experimentalism that the more wild groups do, like those associated with Tatsuya Yoshida, who draws from RIO, zeuhl, and anything else that is just raw chaos.

The Fragments of Resurrection is not chaos, to be sure. The harmonic structures, rhythmic and time changes are all logical, if strange, yet the band stretches. Some chord changes are unusual, and similarly, some rhythmic shifts are more surprising. Sayonaraitsuka draw their sound from unexpected shifts that will catch even jaded math rock listeners as out of nowhere. Wild and random? No. This is not Ruins, yet the sounds and structures are so different from toe, LITE and the others that one thinks of Muddy World, simply because Sayonaraitsuka is so different.

And yet like that band, the present band just does not have much out there, and unfortunately, even finding information is difficult because the band’s name, with a few spellings in transliteration, shares the name of a more popular work in Japanese fiction. So it is that a few of the more interesting experiments extending core sounds in Japanese math rock leave little in the way of recorded legacy.
user_history.review_title: Unique and different Japanese math rock

user_history.review_text:
Tricot is a bit of an oddity among Japanese math rock bands, and an oddity generally. They have a combination of shifting rhythms and time characteristic of math rock, along with a bit of punk, but more of the pop-punk occasionally popular, which risks a kind of bubblegum aesthetic, which the group somehow, amazingly, manages to avoid. More than anything else, that is what astonishes about the group. As is often the case with the Japanese math rock groups, tricot’s albums can be hard to acquire if you want the physical media in the US, with 3 being the most widely available. A N D, released in 2015, and two years before that album, has many of the characteristics of 3, but some notable differences. It is considerably more ragged and less polished, which is to the benefit of the music.

The greatest challenge tricot faces is the risk of bubblegum, and the more elements of raggedness they can include, or put another way, the less sheen they put on the finished product, the more they reduce the risk that the music comes across in any way bubblegum. 3, for all the math rock oddity of angularity, could be heard that way. Its charm, in many ways, came from that contrast, and it is a very good listen, yet if there is anything to recommend A N D above that 2017 album, it is that the slightly lower level of polish reduces the bubblegum component of the recording, allowing the more aggressive elements of the songs, and the angularity of the math rock compositions to play more strongly against the vocals, which cannot help but come across as a bit more saccharine. And thus the tension works even more to the benefit of the group. The rawness, the angularity, and the contrast with the vocals. Fascinating. Strong instrumental work, well contained within the framework of the compositions so as not to be flashy, and allowing the tension within the music to be the star.

It should also be noted that if you get the two disc version, you get a bonus track by an artist who has a style notably similar to tricot. Typing it into the review is difficult because her name uses Japanese characters, but she is quite good, and if you have the option, get that.

Overall, A N D puts the band somewhat closer to Ling Tosite Sigure, and perhaps even some of the Western math rock bands who lean more punk, although certainly not Tatsuya Yoshida. Just that extra bit of an edge, which helps the sound.

user_history.review_text: When considering this entry by Rock In Opposition group, Etron Fou Leloublan, recorded one year before the formal festival itself, some references may help.  It requires no great stretch of the imagination to conjure the image of the following.  Picture a more traditional rock fan hearing Captain Beefheart’s Trout Mask Replica for the first time, back when it was released.  What is this, the hypothetical listener may ask, jazz?  No.  Just Don Van Vliet.  The chaos and disorder would be difficult to distinguish from jazz for one who does not listen to the form, though.  One step further, or closer, depending on one’s frame of mind, is Rock In Opposition.  There is variation in what the various bands did, but Etron Fou Leloublan could get pretty out-there.  Abstract, and while one may hear some aesthetic similarities between Etron Fou Leloublan and some of those challenging earlier rock references, like Don, or Zappa, there really is more jazz in the form here.  Abstract to be sure, hints of free jazz, yet still tethered to rock in strange ways, and one listening to the instrumental work familiar with jazz as it was developing in the 1970s can hear the group building on some of the more adventurous sounds, along with spoken word, hints of Zappa’s hero, Edgard Varese (less well known than his appreciation for Stravinsky, but still important), and all of it showing why the 1978 festival needed to exist.  Les 3 Fous… is one strange album, and even what Zappa was doing around this time wasn’t as out-there.  Univers Zero, for example, put out 1313 the same year, which was still connected to Zappa, Crimson, a bit of Magma, and a few more grounded sounds, although still very adventurous.  They were honing their sound by increments.  Les 3 Fous… is bonkers in the best way.  The old line was, “it has a good beat, you can dance to it,” and if that’s what you want, you probably aren’t reading reviews of Rock In Opposition albums, but Etron Fou Leloublan moves in and out of coherent structures, threatening to decohere, if we can make that a word, at every moment.  Crunching one moment, joyous the next, noisily incomprehensible another.  Yet were that not the case, the tension that gives the music its fascination wouldn’t be there.  France gave a home to ex-pat jazz musicians throughout the 20th Century, when the US did not pay much attention to jazz, or the many geniuses it had produced.  For whatever reason, France saw value, and rightly so.  French jazz does not, and never has merely meant Django Reinhardt, and Etron Fou Leloublan embraced the range of what their country came to hold in trust for the world.  And the full bonkers-ness of trying to combine all of that, in a carnival-esque, madcap mindframe is what one can hear, one year before the actual Rock In Opposition festival, right here.  Don’t expect full coherence.  Find the coherence where it is, and find the tension where the music moves in and out of it.  Joyous, and joyously weird.

product_meta.title: M?moires: Memories Of Django by Angelo Debarre & Tchavolo Schmitt (2004-10-12)

user_history.review_text:
Gypsy jazz is a style that can sound anachronistic if not handled with care. The other risk is showboating. In the hands of two masters like Angelo Debarre and Tchavolo Schmitt, the past comes alive, and rather than showiness, blazing virtuosity.

These tunes will be familiar. Let’s just be blunt about that. And for the typical fan of this style of music, anyone looking at the album might ask, do I really need yet another recording of Nuages? Didn’t Django pretty much get it right? That is, after all, the philosophy of Tchavolo Schmitt, which would beg the question of why this album exists. It exists because someone needs to keep the music alive, and the challenge of keeping it alive without it just sounding like museum re-creations is difficult. Debarre can be, if we are honest, quite showy. Fun, no doubt, but what do you do when you can play? You play. Schmitt is a little different. Highly reverent toward Django, his approach to music is just do it right. Do it tastefully, and do it right. A virtuoso, of course, but he worries less about how fast he plays, and more about getting the right note in the right place. The fan who wants to hear showboating may go for the young hotshots, and there are plenty, but Schmitt is there to remind them about the importance of good taste.

Debarre pushes him a little. He pushes Tchavolo to show off a bit, and to be honest, that’s kind of fun. They’re both showing off, and having fun. Schmitt keeps things meticulous with his eternal reverence for Reinhardt, shared of course by Debarre. Why does this album exist, then? It exists because it’s just fun. Two masters push each other. They get a little showy, and that’s fine! That’s fun! Moreover, they keep each other on track. In some ways, it’s a balancing act where they push each other and check each other in the best of ways. However it comes about, though, it just sounds meticulous, masterful, and fun.

Are there more experimental, modern takes on the form? Sure. Can you find showier players? Yes. But there is something special going on here, with two players who can bring out the best in each other.
user_history.review_title: Two masters bring out the best in each other

target_product.review_text:
Mudy on the sakuban has carved an interesting niche in Japan’s progressive rock scene. There is a point at which one questions whether one is listening to math rock, post rock, or something else, and mudy on the sakuban plays around somewhere in this space, and in such a crowded field, that is to their benefit. As one listens to pavilion, one might especially wonder whether there is any connection between mudy on the sakuban and that great band which released only one album, Muddy World. In fact, there is not, although the name is not the only point of similarity. There are hints of familiarity running throughout the music, even if mudy on the sakuban plays a style much more connected to punk-inflected post rock in a Japanese progressive style than anything else.

Surprisingly, as one counts out the meter, one can find 4/4 rearing its head, although as fans of modern music have come to learn, complex polyrhythms can be used to wrest interesting sounds out of 4/4, and the group exploits similar techniques, even if it is easier to hear the 4/4 than on some groups’ more abstruse efforts. Nevertheless, the math rock elements, as one hears them, come more in the form of playing with tempo and angular melodies rather than rhythmic shifts or complex meters. Moreover, the punk-ish energy is almost reminiscent of Yosowayoso in places, if not as wild. If nothing else, there is more recklessness than tricot or Ling Tosite Sigure, and their incorporation of punk into math rock, while still retaining more form than a Tatsuya Yoshida project like Ruins or Korekyojinn, sets them apart.

In many ways, then, the closest reference point would be someone like Marnie Stern, even if the basic aesthetic is closer to Japanese progressive rock than the U.S. At first blush, one listening to pavilion will hear it as LITE, or a similar group. The layers, though, peel away to reveal, in some ways less, and in some ways, more. Less complex meters, less precision, but more wild, reckless energy.

That is its own charm.
